summary: Gives a roadmap to the BGP-4 documents and reports on implementation experience, building on earlier BGP versions and their use in the connected Internet. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 1773.

eli5.summary: A map telling readers which papers to read to learn BGP, with notes from people who built it. A newer one replaced it.

subtitle: A guide to the documents that define BGP-4 and report on implementation experience.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 is a new version of BGP that supports classless routing, but people need guidance on which documents to read and how it performs in practice.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a roadmap of the BGP-4 specification documents and reports implementation experience from vendors who have built BGP-4.
tldr.outcome: This document was replaced by RFC 1773 as BGP continued to evolve, but it captured important early deployment lessons.

today: RFC 1656 is obsolete and replaced by RFC 1773 as BGP-4 continued to evolve. However, it documents important early implementation experience and design decisions that shaped BGP routing deployments.

sections.title: Introduction to BGP-4
sections.content:
RFC 1656 provides context for Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4), which connects the different Internet regions called Autonomous Systems (ASs). BGP-4 is built on experience from earlier BGP versions and actual use on the Internet.

The key innovation of BGP-4 is support for classless inter-domain routing: it can advertise network blocks of any size, not just the old fixed sizes called "classes." It also supports route aggregation, where many specific routes can be combined into one larger route.
sections.eli5: BGP is how different Internet regions tell each other how to reach different parts of the network. BGP-4 is a newer version that is more flexible than the old way.

sections.title: Implementations and Testing
sections.content:
By 1994, four vendors had independently built BGP-4: ANS, Europanet, 3COM, and Cisco. The RFC describes testing of one implementation in a lab network that mimicked the complexity of real Internet borders, including routing information from major backbone networks like Alternet, EBone and Sprint.

Testing confirmed that BGP-4 could carry CIDR prefixes (both larger and smaller network blocks), aggregate routes using AS set aggregation, and use new features like LOCAL_PREF to influence route selection within an AS.
sections.eli5: Four companies built BGP-4, and engineers tested it in a pretend network that looked like the real Internet to make sure it worked.

sections.title: Key Observations
sections.content:
All implementations could exchange network reachability information. However, not all could automatically create aggregate routes from more specific ones. The RFC notes that while deaggregation (breaking aggregates back into individual routes) is possible, it can cause dangerous routing explosions if not tightly controlled.

The RFC also observes that automatic version negotiation between BGP speakers is risky: packet losses or restarts might cause two BGP-4 speakers to accidentally negotiate an older BGP version that cannot handle supernets and subnets, breaking the deployment.
sections.eli5: Everyone could send and receive routes, but not everyone could combine them. Trying to undo combinations can break things.
